## Motivation {.section-title}

Motherhood is conceptualised dichotomously in the labour-market penalty
literature: women either have no children — a role perceived as relatively
compatible with high expectations of work devotion — or they are mothers.

This study treats motherhood as **bidimensional**. Women may be evaluated not
only in relation to their current parental status, but also in relation to
their **potential fertility**: the expectation that a person will have a child
in the near future.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Potential fertility applies to men and women, with or without children.
:::

---

## Why the distinction matters theoretically

Motherhood stereotypes concern **current performance and costs already
incurred**. Potential fertility concerns **assumptions about future
behaviour**.

If the two operate through different mechanisms, they should leave different
signatures across evaluation dimensions:

| Dimension | Motherhood | Potential fertility |
|---|---|---|
| Perceived cost | expected | expected |
| Perceived risk | expected | expected |
| Growth potential | expected | expected |
| **Current competence** | **expected** | **not expected** |

The competence dimension is where the two accounts diverge. This is the
prediction the design is built to test.

---

## Research question

> What stereotypes do employers associate with the potential fertility and the
> motherhood of labour-market-active women in Chile?

Specific questions for this talk:

- Is there a "pure" gender penalty?
- Is there a "pure" motherhood penalty?
  - Is this penalty gendered?
- Is there a future motherhood penalty?
  - Is this penalty gendered?
- Is there an additional child penalty (among mothers)?
  - Is this penalty gendered?


::: {.footer-note}
Preregistered at AsPredicted #297542 prior to data collection.
:::

# Design {.section-divider}

---

## Why a factorial survey

The phenomenon is based on **expectations and assumptions about the future**,
which makes it difficult to observe directly. Because it concerns
discrimination, direct questioning induces social-desirability bias.

Factorial surveys experimentally manipulate a fictional scenario, which allows
control over all attributes and causal identification of the effect of each on
an evaluation outcome.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Design**

- Vignette-based, rating outcomes
- D-efficient fractional design
- 200 unique profiles, 100 blocks of 2
- Each block assigned to 8 respondents
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Efficiency**

- D-efficiency = 0.922
- G-efficiency = 0.925
:::
:::

---

## Manipulated attributes

Respondents evaluate applicants for a vacancy presented by a fictional human
resources firm. Six attributes vary at the profile level:

| Attribute | Levels |
|---|---|
| Gender | woman / man |
| Marital status | single / married |
| Parental status | no children / one child / two children |
| Family plans | in 2 years / in 5 years / does not want children |
| Experience | 6 / 7 / 8 years |
| Performance on a technical test | 5.8 / 6.0 / 6.3 |

Potential fertility is signalled by the **family plans** attribute, crossed
with parental status. This separates current motherhood from anticipated
fertility as distinct experimental factors.

---

## Between- and within-subject structure

**Occupational level is between-subjects.** Each respondent evaluates profiles
of either professional or technical applicants only, with no overlap.

Each respondent evaluates **two profiles** ($n_d = 2$) drawn from one
pre-generated block, sequentially and independently.

Presentation order and template version are recorded and controlled in all
models.

---

## Sample

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
| | Professional | Technical |
|---|---|---|
| Profile observations | 1,454 | 1,444 |
| Respondents | 727 | 722 |
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Target population: supervisory and managerial workers in Chile.

Fielded through Netquest. Sample size constrained by maximum panel
availability.
:::
:::

Attention checks applied by the panel provider before delivery. A
task-specific attention check is included; the preregistered protocol analyses
the full and restricted samples and reports a sensitivity comparison.

---

## Outcomes

**9 items**, all on 7-point scales. Third-order evaluations.

- Hiring recommendation
- Competence index (2 items: capable and trustworthy)
- Good investment
- Growth index (promising, ambitious, take on new challenges, be
  promoted)
- Risk index (committed long-term, arrive late or be absent, resign, risky for continuity)
- Operationally costly
- Likelihood of requesting accommodations
- Likelihood of using company benefits


::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Preregistered decision rule.** Items aggregate into indices where Cronbach's
$\alpha \geq .70$; otherwise they are analysed individually.
:::

---

## Applying the aggregation rule

| Construct | Items | $\alpha$ | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Risk | 3 | .756 | aggregated |
| Growth potential | 4 | .837 | aggregated |
| Competence | 3 | .807 | aggregated |
| **Cost** | 4 | **.631** | **analysed by item** |

The cost construct did not meet the threshold. Following the preregistered
rule, its four items are reported individually rather than forced into an
index.

::: {.footer-note}
All individual item analyses are reported regardless of whether indices are used.
:::

---

## Estimation

**OLS with cluster-robust standard errors (CR2), clustered by respondent.**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Why not multilevel**

The D-efficient design already includes each manipulated attribute as a fixed
effect. With $n_d = 2$ profiles per respondent, random slopes are not
identified and nesting on anything other than respondent is unstable.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Why CR2**

Bias-reduced linearisation with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
[@pustejovsky2018]. With ~1,449 clusters, well outside the small-sample
regime; realised $df$ range 430–1,090.
:::
:::

Twelve preregistered model sets: main effects, gender interactions with
parental status, family plans and marital status, three-way combinations, and
occupational-level moderation.

---

## Reporting quantities

Attributes are coded with **sum contrasts**, so coefficients are deviations
from the design mean rather than differences from an arbitrary reference level.

Results are reported as **marginal means and contrasts** rather than
coefficients:

- Differences in coefficients across subgroups are sensitive to reference
  category, producing subgroup comparisons of arbitrary sign, size and
  significance [@leeper2020]
- Marginal means are estimated by G-computation over the observed sample rather
  than a balanced grid, which keeps every estimate within the support of the
  D-efficient design

Gender moderation is tested as a **difference-in-differences** with its own
standard error, not by comparing significance across subgroups.

# Results {.section-divider}

---

## Pooling across occupational conditions

Preregistered moderation tests (SETS 5a–5e) find no evidence that occupational
level conditions the focal effects.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Gender × occupation: no coefficient exceeds $|0.052|$ across 16 outcomes
- Confidence bounds exclude moderation greater than **0.14 scale points**
- Direct heterogeneity test across arms: Cochran $Q = 306.2$, $df = 285$,
  $p = .185$
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Pooling reduces standard errors by **29%**.

Results below are pooled, with occupational level as a control. By-condition
estimates are reported in the appendix.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**Exception:** H16 is reported by condition. Marriage effects among parents
diverge significantly across arms ($p_{het} < .01$ on four outcomes).
:::

---

## The baseline gender contrast

| Outcome | Contrast | $\Delta$ P(rated 6–7) |
|---|---|---|
| Expected: request accommodations | +0.49*** | +11.8 pts |
| Expected: late or absent | +0.47*** | +7.7 pts |
| Risky for job continuity | +0.39*** | +5.2 pts |
| Expected: quit | +0.28*** | +4.1 pts |
| Hiring recommendation | −0.05 | −3.1 pts |
| Competence index | +0.04 | — |
| Growth potential index | −0.03 | — |

Evaluations of competence, growth potential and hiring do not differ by gender.
Predicted conduct differs substantially.

Childless women, plans in 2 years vs. no plans:

## Do men experience a future fatherhood penalty?

Difference-in-differences: the 2-year contrast for women minus the same
contrast for men.

| Outcome | Women − men | $q$ |
|---|---|---|
| Expected: quit | +0.62*** | <.001 |
| Risk index | +0.50*** | <.001 |
| Risky for continuity | +0.44** | .007 |
| Expected: late or absent | +0.43** | .006 |
| Committed long-term | −0.29** | .016 |
| Hiring recommendation | −0.19* | .045 |

The 5-year difference-in-differences is null on all 19 outcomes.

# Discussion {.section-divider}

---

## What the results indicate

**Evaluators produce equivalent bottom-line judgments while holding
differentiated expectations about conduct.** The gender difference appears in
predicted behaviour — absence, accommodations, continuity risk, quitting — and
not in competence, growth potential or hiring recommendation.

**The penalty attaches to anticipated fertility rather than to motherhood as
such.** The 2-year horizon carries the penalty; the 5-year horizon largely does
not. Once a woman has children, stating further plans adds less than it does
for childless women.

**Motherhood and potential fertility leave different signatures.** Motherhood
at two children moves both conduct and growth-potential measures; the gender
contrast alone moves only conduct.

---

## Limitations

- Occupational level is between-subjects, so the occupational main effect
  confounds the profile contrast with any composition difference between the
  two respondent samples. Balance checks across arms are pending.
- Realised sample is approximately 9% below the preregistered target per arm.
- Design attributes explain a modest share of variance ($R^2$ median 0.022),
  as is typical for factorial surveys with this number of manipulated
  attributes.
- The technical condition is an occupational-credential contrast, not a
  class-position measure.

---

## Next steps

**Committed in the preregistration, pending**

- Attention-check sensitivity analysis: full vs. restricted sample
- Unadjusted marginal means alongside the model-adjusted estimates
- Omnibus $F$-test for the pooling decision, in place of the heterogeneity test
  reported here

**Robustness**

- Ordered-probit estimation for the seven outcomes exceeding 20% at ceiling
- Formal test of the conduct-versus-evaluation dissociation, by stacking
  outcomes and interacting attributes with outcome type — currently supported by
  comparison across separate models rather than by a single estimate
- Preregistered secondary analyses: moderation by evaluator gender, parental
  status, hiring experience and workplace-norm attitudes

---

## An open measurement question {.section-title}

For childless women, stating plans to have children in 2 years reduces the
probability of a top-two-box competence rating by **16.9 points**, while the
mean shifts by −0.05 ($p = .41$).

The distributional and mean-based results disagree, on the outcome with the
highest ceiling concentration in the design.

This bears directly on how ordinal evaluation scales should be analysed in
factorial surveys, and is the first thing I intend to resolve.

::: {.footer-note}
$n = 323$ observations, 279 respondents. Unadjusted contrast; the
model-adjusted comparison is pending.
:::
